hook.text: Three generations under one roof: grandparents, parents, children, and cousins. In much of the world, this is normal.

buildup.text: Extended families include multiple generations and relatives living together or in close proximity, sharing resources.

discovery.text: They provide built-in childcare, elder care, economic support, and social insurance that the nuclear family lacks.

twist.text: Extended families can be restrictive. Freedom, privacy, and personal choice are often sacrificed for the group.

climax.text: Extended families trade individual freedom for collective security. They're resilient but demand conformity.

punchline.text: More family means more support and more rules.

quiz.question: What advantage do extended families provide?
options: Built-in childcare, elder care, and economic support

details.summary: Extended families include multiple generations and collateral relatives living together or in close proximity. They pool labor, share childcare, and provide mutual support in ways that nuclear families cannot replicate independently.
details.whyItMatters: Extended families are the most common household form across human history and remain prevalent globally. They provide economic resilience, elder care, and child-rearing support that industrialized societies increasingly struggle to replace.
takeaways: Extended families include multiple generations under one roof or nearby
They pool labor, share childcare, and provide mutual economic support
This family form is the historical norm across most human societies

faq.question: Why are extended families more common in agrarian societies?
faq.answer: Farming requires labor that a single couple cannot provide alone. Extended families offer a built-in workforce, shared childcare, and risk pooling. Land-based economies benefit from keeping family members together to work shared property across generations.

faq.question: Are extended families declining in the modern world?
faq.answer: Urbanization and wage labor have reduced extended family households in many countries. However, they remain strong in much of Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. Economic crises can also revive multigenerational living even in Western countries.
